extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and readers interested in the evolutionary origins of humor and laughter (evolutionary psychologists, humor researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Judging a theoretical account (book) of the evolution and function of humor: its explanatory power, empirical support, scope across humor types, and readability/scholarly contribution. Focus is on whether the proposed cognitive/reward mechanisms plausibly explain humor and laughter and can be empirically tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of adaptive function / ultimate mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must explain the adaptive function of humor and laughter — i.e., whether the cognitive mechanism described actually accounts for why humor evolved and how it contributed to survival/reproduction. (Quoted: “The ultimate question is whether the cognitive mechanism described by the authors explains the adaptive function of humor and laughter.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show necessity and sufficiency: demonstrate that humor provides adaptive benefits beyond trivial effects, explain how it affects fitness, and address whether other cognitive mechanisms already handle serious errors. Offer clear argumentation and empirical or logical support rather than speculative assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and specificity of proposed reward system
rubrics_metrics.description: If humor is claimed to be a sexually selected trait, the account must posit a strongly supported reward system that justifies selection (authors: reward system built on the error debugging mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the nature of the reward (e.g., fitness enhancement via mate choice rather than merely subjective error-reduction pleasure), connect it to measurable physiological/behavioral markers (e.g., Duchenne laughter), and consider alternative reward mechanisms. Explicitly link the proposed reward to selection pressures and observable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and coverage across humor forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must cover not only set-up/punch-line jokes but also other forms of humor (e.g., ironic statements, conversational sarcasm, first-person self-deprecating moments). (Reviewer notes irony is not discussed: “a simple ironic statement ... is not dependent on a covert belief which is then falsified”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how the mechanism applies (or explain its limits) for non-joke humor such as irony, sarcasm, conversational quips, fables, and fictional incongruities. Avoid limiting the account to a narrow class of jokes without addressing common everyday humor types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative use of examples and generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (jokes, anecdotes) used to illustrate the theory should be representative and support general claims rather than only fitting the theory post-hoc. (Reviewer: “Inside Jokes uses jokes primarily as examples to verify their theory.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diverse, cross-cultural, and non-scripted examples; test whether examples that seem to fit are genuinely diagnostic versus cherry-picked. Show generalization beyond classic set-up/punch-line structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testable hypotheses and empirical corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should generate clear, testable hypotheses and be open to empirical verification, especially using neuroscience and experimental methods. (Reviewer: “The theory offers some clear hypotheses that could be corroborated with future studies, especially with the advances of research in neuroscience.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific predictions, operationalize constructs (e.g., what counts as 'debugging' or the relevant reward signal), and propose feasible experimental or neuroscientific tests. Indicate what evidence would falsify the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with sexual selection and mating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that humor evolved via sexual selection must align with empirical data on sex differences in humor ability, signaling, reception, and mating success (e.g., higher male humor ability, humor predicting mating outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare theoretical claims to existing empirical studies, quantify effect sizes where possible, and explain any mismatches or complexities (e.g., women's choosiness, differential costs/benefits). Avoid inferring strong sexual-selection conclusions without corroborating data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of claimed mechanism with observed laughter intensity/quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should account for different intensities/qualities of mirth and laughter (e.g., first-person humor is often weak and not accompanied by Duchenne laughter), and link these to the proposed reward mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between kinds of laughter (Duchenne vs. non-Duchenne), measure mirth intensity across contexts, and show that the reward mechanism predicts when strong versus weak laughter occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of overgeneralization / realistic scope claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The account should not over-extend by claiming humor is necessary for preventing fatal mistakes or that it uniquely provides functions that other cognitive mechanisms do not already serve. (Reviewer: many serious mistakes are handled by other non-funny mechanisms.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about the bounds of the theory: specify which cognitive problems humor plausibly addresses (e.g., minor incongruities) and avoid grand claims unsupported by evidence. Discuss alternative mechanisms and how humor complements them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of fictional and trivial incongruities
rubrics_metrics.description: Because humor often involves trivial or fictional incongruities (e.g., fables), a theory must explain why such non-literal or non-real errors produce mirth and apparent reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address how mental simulation, narrative fiction, or play contexts modulate the proposed mechanism; include examples of fictional incongruities and show how they map onto the cognitive account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, accessibility, and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition should be clear and well organized for the intended audience; excessive tangential footnotes or highly technical sections may impede non-expert readers. (Reviewer: writing is clear and eloquent though some footnotes are too tangential; chapter 7 may be difficult for non-experts.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance scholarly depth with readability: keep asides and footnotes relevant, signpost technical sections, and provide summaries or intuitive explanations for non-specialists. Tailor complexity to audience or provide layered explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical originality and comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should contribute original, comprehensive theorizing to the literature on humor evolution (this book is noted as one of the most complex and sophisticated theories presented and the first book devoted entirely to the evolution of humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight novel mechanisms or integrative syntheses, show how the theory advances beyond prior accounts, and map out remaining open questions for future research.
